binders: p(x,t) and u(x,t) are the two unknown fields, depending on one spatial coordinate x and time t; the passage does not specify their precise domains or explicitly state quantifiers (raw PDF page 24, equation (1.5) and its explanatory paragraph).

K and ρ are fixed material constants; c is defined from them by c = √(K/ρ), rather than introduced as an unrelated free parameter (raw PDF page 24, paragraph following (1.5) and definition following (1.6)).
hypotheses: The fields satisfy p_t + K u_x = 0 and u_t + (1/ρ)p_x = 0 (raw PDF page 24, equation (1.5)).
The medium is one-dimensional and has constant K and ρ (raw PDF page 24, introduction to (1.5) and paragraph identifying the material constants).
conclusions: The scalar field w¹ = p + ρcu satisfies w¹_t + c w¹_x = 0 (raw PDF page 24, first transformation and transport equation following (1.6)).
The scalar field w² = p − ρcu satisfies w²_t − c w²_x = 0 (raw PDF page 24, second transformation and final transport equation).

These two scalar equations constitute a decomposition of system (1.5) into two distinct acoustic waves traveling in opposite directions, with speeds +c and −c (raw PDF page 25, opening sentence; raw PDF page 24, directional interpretations of the scalar equations).
definitions_and_conventions: p denotes pressure, more precisely perturbation from a constant background pressure; u denotes particle velocity (raw PDF page 24, paragraph following (1.5)).
K denotes bulk modulus of compressibility and ρ denotes density (raw PDF page 24, paragraph following (1.5)).
q = (p,u) as a column vector and A = [[0,K],[1/ρ,0]], so the coupled equations have the form q_t + A q_x = 0 (raw PDF page 24, equation (1.6) and preceding text).
c = √(K/ρ) is the sound speed, and ρc is the coefficient multiplying u in each scalar combination (raw PDF page 24, displays and prose following (1.6)).

Superscripts 1 and 2 label the two scalar fields; subscripts t and x denote partial differentiation, as used in their displayed equations (raw PDF page 24, definitions of w¹ and w² and their transport equations).
implicit_context: The discussion uses a positive sound speed: the preceding one-way model explicitly has c > 0, and the two acoustic combinations are interpreted as distinct rightward and leftward waves. Separate inequalities K > 0 and ρ > 0 are not explicitly written on these pages (raw PDF page 24, introduction to (1.4) and acoustic transformation; raw PDF page 25, opening sentence).

Sufficient differentiability for the displayed first partial derivatives and their linear combinations is implicit in the assertion that the transformed fields satisfy the equations; no function space or weak-solution convention is supplied (raw PDF page 24, equation (1.5) and verification assertion following (1.6)).

The surrounding explanation places this acoustic decomposition within hyperbolic constant-coefficient systems, whose eigenvectors permit unique state decomposition and whose eigenvalues give wave speeds; the acoustic eigenvalues are −c and +c (raw PDF page 25, opening paragraph).

details: The input is a pair of coupled pressure–velocity equations, and the output consists of two separate scalar transport equations (raw PDF page 24, (1.5) and the two transformed equations; raw PDF page 25, opening sentence).
Both combinations are part of the claim: retaining only one would omit one of the two acoustic directions (raw PDF page 25, opening sentence specifying two distinct waves).
The plus combination p + ρcu corresponds to coefficient +c in the transport equation; the minus combination p − ρcu corresponds to coefficient −c (raw PDF page 24, displays following (1.6)).
Positive c denotes sound speed; +c corresponds to rightward motion and −c to leftward motion (raw PDF page 24, explanation of (1.4) and final paragraph).
The source calls the construction a decomposition of the system, not merely a single consequence of it (raw PDF page 25, opening sentence).

Analyst inference: when ρc ≠ 0, the displayed combinations recover p = (w¹+w²)/2 and u = (w¹−w²)/(2ρc), supporting the interpretation as a full change of variables. These inverse formulas are not printed in the selected passage (raw PDF page 24, definitions of w¹ and w²; raw PDF page 25, decomposition assertion).

Preserve the pairing of w¹ with +c and w² with −c, and the conclusion that both directional waves occur (raw PDF page 24, transformed equations; raw PDF page 25, opening sentence).
Treat K and ρ as constants for this statement (raw PDF page 24, paragraph following (1.5)).

contract_plain_english: For the one-dimensional acoustic system p_t + K u_x = 0 and u_t + (1/ρ)p_x = 0 with constant material parameters, define c = √(K/ρ). The combinations w¹ = p + ρcu and w² = p − ρcu satisfy scalar transport equations with coefficients +c and −c, respectively (raw PDF page 24, equation (1.5) and displays following (1.6)). The source identifies this as a decomposition into two distinct acoustic waves traveling in opposite directions at the sound speed (raw PDF page 25, opening sentence). Precise regularity and parameter inequalities are implicit rather than formally enumerated in the displayed source.
